t: A Radical Way To Transform Difficult Students https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/04/29/a-radical-way-to-transform-difficult-students/
q: You spend more time dealing with them than any ten students put together. You think about them in your off hours. You talk about them with your spouse.
Well, the big secret is that they know how you feel about them, even if you've done your Meryl-Streep best pretending otherwise.
Children are astute, even psychic, judges of how adults perceive them. Far more than we give them credit for.
When there is an absence of mutual likability between you and your most challenging students, you lose nearly all of your leverage to influence their behavior.
You make a conscious decision that, no matter what they do or how they behave or how many times they disrupt your class, you’re going to see only the best in them.
It triggers the Law of Reciprocity and causes in them a desire to please you and behave for you.

The intervention is a deliberate, effortful mental choice to see only the best in the student, not a spontaneous feeling.

t: Why Staying Late After School Is A Mistake
q: It makes them feel as if they’re doing everything they can for their students.
Because staying late after school doesn’t make you a better teacher. It makes you worse.
You need to be rested and refreshed before greeting your students each morning. You need to be clear-eyed and quick thinking, patient and observant.
Parkinson’s Law is the tendency to expand a task in complexity and importance in relation to the time given for its completion.
The law also states that when you give yourself less time you become more focused. Your concentration increases.
They end up with lessons that are bloated and directionless and that students struggle to understand.
Set a deadline, say half or two-thirds the amount of time you usually stay after school, then stick with it. Turn out the lights. Close the door. Walk swiftly to your car without looking back.
x: Linsin argues that staying late at school, whether out of pride, guilt, or overwhelm, ultimately makes teachers worse at their jobs rather than better.
Long hours after school do not make a teacher more effective.

He contends that effectiveness in the classroom depends on being rested, clear-eyed, and patient each morning, and that chronic overwork erodes those qualities even when teachers insist they can handle it.
Parkinson's Law explains why open-ended prep time gets wasted — work expands to fill whatever time is allotted.
Giving yourself less time to plan increases focus and reduces the chance for distraction, uncertainty, and inefficiency.

q: I've held more than a few pop-up debates that went badly, and I could trace the badness back to before the debate started. What am I talking about? The Plague of the Poorly Formulated Pop-Up Debate Prompt.
Well, true — but then it wouldn't be Romeo and Juliet either. If arguing one of the sides requires such drastic measures, it's not defensible to the degree we want it to be for a good pop-up debate.

But the trouble is that it can quickly get off track based on how we define “barbaric.” On the one hand, if we're defining barbaric as “savagely cruel and exceedingly brutal,” as Google's first definition does, then this is really a question of comparing the severity of their actions to those of contemporary societies.

If you can Google your debatable prompt and absolutely nothing comes up, that might be a sign that almost no one on the planet really argues about what you are prompting. As I recall, this debate was a bit yawny — authenticity is one of the reasons why.

If I were to tell my students at the start of the year that we'd be having a big debate about who was most responsible for the Cold War, the USA or the USSR, only the history nerds would be excited. But by the time we finish studying the Cold War, kids are into the pop-up debate because they know a lot about the topic.

t: When And Why It's Okay For Students To Talk
q: There is a common misconception that effective classroom management means silence.
It causes boredom, resentment, and a strong dislike for school. It makes every day an agonizing, tension-filled slog to dismissal.
To create a healthy, well-behaved environment, your students need breaks. They need opportunities to stretch their legs and recharge their batteries.
Now, it’s important to point out that letting students continue to talk because that’s what they’re already doing is a bad idea and will only make matters worse.
You lay out your expectations by showing precisely what is and isn’t okay. A reminder that you’ll follow your classroom management plan as usual is also a good idea.
Giving students a few minutes to talk with their friends is a simple little thing. But it effectively shakes the restlessness out of their system.
It settles. It calms. It motivates. It prepares them for the challenges that lie ahead.
x: Constant, rigid silence is not the same as good classroom management.
Constant, rigid silence is not the same as good classroom management — it causes boredom, resentment, and dislike of school.
He distinguishes between necessary quiet periods, such as independent work, and the rest of the day, when students need built-in breaks to recharge.
The talking break must be defined and demonstrated by the teacher first — letting ongoing chatter continue only makes things worse.
Constant, rigid silence is not the same as good classroom management.
Structured, teacher-modeled talking breaks of two to four minutes are one of the most effective ways to reset student energy.
Linsin pushes back on the idea that good classroom management requires constant silence, arguing that rigid quiet only breeds boredom, resentment, and a dislike of school.

t: Relationships: Not a Separate Goal, but a Fruit of and a Means to the Goal
q: When people set off on a Mount Everest trek (says the guy who has, of course, done this many times), they don't spend an hour doing relationship-building games, or multiple hours creating “This is Who I Am” projects. Instead, they set off on the trek, and as the peak comes into view, their sense of community coheres around that shared, daunting, thrilling goal. They develop relationships as a byproduct of working toward this challenging thing together.

So I don't really budget class time for the developing of relationships. Even our very first activity is just as much about introducing argumentative claims as it is relationship-building, and that's about as ice-breakery as it gets. No multi-day autobiographical activities — we just dive into the work, no big sharing time.

But relationships aren't the objective in any of this stuff — they are the byproducts of the big objective, of us getting closer together as Everest comes into view. Front and center during those first weeks, I'm trying to communicate, in any way that I can, who we are and what we're working toward.

In the AP class for ninth graders, we're working toward not just a test in May during which the odds say we're supposed to fail — we're also working toward becoming the kind of people who flourish long-term. In the non-AP class, we're working toward mastering world history.

We're all on the same team, in the same family, working toward the same, important thing: becoming the best people we can be. And along the way, the relationships come: in all their joy and mess and substance and utility and goodness.
x: Using the image of a Mount Everest trek, he claims community forms as a byproduct of pursuing a shared, daunting goal together, not through ice-breakers or autobiographical projects.
Stuart skips multi-day ice-breaker and autobiography activities and starts with real academic work from the first activity.
The choice between relationships and curriculum is a false one, because relationships are a byproduct of working together toward a hard goal.
His emphasis in the early weeks is communicating who the class is and what it is working toward.

t: How To Handle Students Who Misbehave Behind Your Back hind-your-back/
q: You know there were students misbehaving. You know there were students off task and taking advantage of a moment when your back was turned.
But you hesitate to enforce a consequence because you aren't absolutely sure. Plus, they know you didn't see them, which could embolden them to lie and deny.
But this is a remarkably stressful approach that risks building a wall of resentment with students who may or may not even be guilty.
It takes pretending that you didn’t even notice their misbehavior.
You see, if at first you do nothing at all, if you show no reaction or change in routine or behavior, it’s a surefire guarantee that they’re going to do it again—usually within seconds.
You'll have them dead to rights and be able to enforce a consequence without stress, drama, or the prospect of having to prove their misbehavior.
It’s your job to see misbehavior, to protect every student’s right to learn and enjoy school. Vigilant supervision is a prerequisite of effective classroom management.
x: Linsin addresses the frustrating situation where a teacher senses misbehavior happening just out of view but lacks the certainty needed to act.
Linsin addresses the frustrating situation where a teacher senses misbehavior happening just out of view but lacks the certainty needed to act.
Confronting suspected students without certainty risks punishing the innocent and building resentment without resolving anything.
Pretending not to notice, then using peripheral vision and positioning, lets a teacher catch the behavior directly on the next attempt.
Students who misbehave out of view will almost always repeat the behavior again within seconds if the teacher shows no reaction.
Catching students in the act allows a consequence to be delivered without stress, drama, or the need to prove guilt.
Vigilant supervision — not confrontation or threats — is what protects every student's right to learn and enjoy school.

q: There are thousands of ways to be a great, master teacher, but there is really only one way to be a bad one.
This is the critical juncture: the moment when you realize a negative difference between how you expected things to go, and how they are actually going.
It's not a one-time thing — we are constantly coming upon these fork-in-the-road moments when the essays are terrible or the quizzes are bombed or the workload is unmanageable.
This is the less frequently travelled road because it means we have to detach our sense of self-worth from our results or our performance.
Part of becoming a master teacher is learning when to disengage at the critical juncture and when to dig in.
But if the path of disengagement becomes the default, we all end up at the same old place: burn-out, boredom, complaint, excuse.
On the other hand, strategic engagement at the critical juncture takes us down diverse roads to diverse places.
x: The framing asymmetry is the hook and the argument: many routes to great teaching, essentially one route to bad teaching, and it runs through how one recurring moment is handled.
Naming the critical juncture at multiple scales, career, year, unit and lesson, makes it recognisable in the small daily instances rather than only in a crisis.

His most useful move is to show that it operates at every scale, career level around year two, year level around October, and right down to a single unit or lesson when the essays are terrible or the quizzes are bombed.
The honest cost of engagement is stated plainly: it requires detaching self-worth from results, which is why the disengagement road is the more travelled one.
He names that moment the critical juncture, the point at which a teacher registers a gap between how they expected things to go and how they are actually going.
The named endpoint of habitual disengagement, burn-out, boredom, complaint and excuse, connects a moment-by-moment choice to the profession's familiar attrition pattern.

t: How To Change A Student's Life
q: You’ll have the trust and likability that breaks down walls and frees them to be themselves around you.
It’s an ability that can change lives, sometimes dramatically, and set a student on a new and better and often redemptive course they never would have found on their own.
As a freshman in high school, I was lost and disillusioned. I was a Gordian knot of shyness and fear and in profound need of direction.
I always have enjoyed finding the students who were good but didn’t know they were good and challenge them to push themselves up.
He saw something in me no one else was able to see, including myself, and it changed me forever.
Exceptional classroom management allows you to build the kind of trusting relationships that reveal who your students are and the unique gifts they can offer the world.
It liberates their abilities lying dormant within, which bubble to the surface and then burst forth in a bright, glowing supernova you can’t help but recognize.
